## High school academics

Here are the independent variables we are exploring;

- `pseo.participant`
- `took.ACT`
- `ACTCompositeScore`
- `ap.exam`
- `MCA.M`
- `MCA.R`
- `MCA.S`
- `cte.achievement`
- `total.cte.courses.taken`

### Summary

Across the high school accomplishments domain, CTE engagement emerges as the most consequential and consistently differentiated predictor of labor market attachment among non-completers. Both CTE achievement level and total CTE courses taken show the strongest effects in the variable set. CTE Concentrators/Completors experience persistently disconnected rates nearly 15 points lower than those with no CTE involvement (40.9% vs. 56.1%), and total CTE courses taken is the only continuous variable for which every pairwise group contrast is significant — indicating a true dose-response relationship across the full disconnection spectrum. This finding is especially salient for Southeast Minnesota, where applied and technical career pathways are embedded in the regional labor market.

Among academic achievement measures, ACT composite score shows the largest effect (F=70.6), with persistently disconnected students scoring roughly 1.4 points below consistently attached peers. ACT participation itself is also protective, with persistently disconnected rates of 42.4% among test-takers versus 49.8% among non-takers — likely proxying broader academic engagement. MCA Math follows a consistent and significant gradient, though pairwise differences are modest in magnitude and most concentrated between the persistently disconnected group and others. MCA Reading reaches omnibus significance but only meaningfully distinguishes the persistently disconnected from the middle two categories in pairwise terms. MCA Science is non-significant at both the omnibus and pairwise levels, the only academic measure to fail entirely.

The two college-access variables present an interpretive caution. AP exam participation shows a paradoxical overrepresentation of persistently disconnected students (51.9% vs. 46.5% overall), and PSEO participation is a null predictor (p=.067). For non-completers, these markers likely reflect interrupted college trajectories rather than workforce readiness — students who signaled college intent in high school but did not sustain enrollment, and who subsequently experienced greater, not lesser, labor market difficulty.

Taken together, the high school accomplishments domain reinforces that career and technical education depth — not college-preparatory signaling — is the strongest in-school protective factor against persistent disconnection for this population.

<br>

::: panel-tabset
### `pseo.participant`

PSEO participation shows no statistically significant relationship with disconnection category (χ²=7.2, df=3, p=.067, Cramer's V=0.018). The distribution across categories is nearly identical for PSEO participants and non-participants, with persistently disconnected rates of 44.8% and 46.3%, respectively. Like AP exam-taking, PSEO enrollment may carry a similar selection paradox for non-completers, but here even that signal does not reach significance. PSEO participation is effectively a null predictor of disconnection persistence in this population.

```{r}
tab_xtab(var.row = master$disconnected.cat, var.col = master$pseo.participant, 
         title = "", 
         show.exp = TRUE,
         show.col.prc = TRUE,
         use.viewer = TRUE,
         file = "Data/Claude/analysis_non_college_deeper/High school accomplishments/pseo-participant.html")
```

### `took.ACT`

ACT test-taking is associated with lower persistent disconnection. Among those who took the ACT, 42.4% were persistently disconnected, compared to 49.8% among those who did not — a meaningful 7-point gap. Consistently attached rates were also higher among ACT-takers (18.4% vs. 14.5%). The association is statistically significant (χ²=201.8, p\<.001) with a small effect size (Cramer's V=0.078). ACT participation likely proxies academic engagement and college orientation rather than reflecting test performance per se.

```{r}
tab_xtab(var.row = master$disconnected.cat, var.col = master$took.ACT, 
         title = "", 
         show.exp = TRUE,
         show.col.prc = TRUE,
         use.viewer = TRUE,
         file = "Data/Claude/analysis_non_college_deeper/High school accomplishments/took-ACT.html")
```

### `ACTCompositeScore`

ACT composite scores differ significantly across disconnection categories (F=70.6, p\<.001), with a clear and graded pattern. Persistently disconnected students scored approximately 1.41 points lower than consistently attached peers (Tukey estimate=−1.41, p\<.001), and even intermittently disconnected students scored about 0.43 points lower (p=.001). The gap between broadly and intermittently disconnected groups is not significant (estimate=0.23, p=.29), suggesting the score gradient flattens in the middle categories and is most pronounced at the poles. The ANOVA residual df of \~14,683 reflects the subset who actually took the ACT.

```{r}
summary <- aov(ACTCompositeScore ~ disconnected.cat, data = master)

summary

anova_df <- broom::tidy(summary)

TukeyHSD(summary)

tukey_df <- broom::tidy(TukeyHSD(summary))

wb <- createWorkbook()
addWorksheet(wb, "ANOVA")
addWorksheet(wb, "TukeyHSD")
writeData(wb, "ANOVA", anova_df)
writeData(wb, "TukeyHSD", tukey_df)
saveWorkbook(wb, "Data/Claude/analysis_non_college_deeper/High school accomplishments/ACTCompositeScore.xlsx", overwrite = TRUE)
```

### `ap.exam`

AP exam participation is modestly associated with disconnection outcomes (χ²=45.5, p\<.001, Cramer's V=0.037), though the effect is small. Notably, persistently disconnected students are overrepresented among AP exam-takers relative to expectation (51.9% observed vs. 46.5% overall), while consistently attached students are slightly underrepresented (13.4% vs. 16.2%). This counterintuitive pattern likely reflects a selection artifact: AP participants in this non-completer sample may have started college but left, leaving them with high school academic markers but without credential attainment — and subsequently experiencing worse labor market attachment.

```{r}
tab_xtab(var.row = master$disconnected.cat, var.col = master$ap.exam, 
         title = "", 
         show.exp = TRUE,
         show.col.prc = TRUE,
         use.viewer = TRUE,
         file = "Data/Claude/analysis_non_college_deeper/High school accomplishments/ap-exam.html")
```

### `MCA.M`

MCA Math scores are significantly associated with disconnection category (F=19.9, p\<.001), with a consistent negative gradient — higher disconnection corresponds to lower math performance. Persistently disconnected students scored approximately 0.13 scale points below consistently attached peers (Tukey estimate=−0.130, p\<.001), and intermittently disconnected students scored about 0.06 points lower (p=.017). The broadly vs. intermittently disconnected contrast is not significant (estimate=−0.026, p=.63), and the persistently vs. broadly disconnected contrast falls just short of significance (p=.082), indicating the gradient is clearest between the persistently disconnected group and the rest.

```{r}
summary <- aov(MCA.M ~ disconnected.cat, data = master)

summary

anova_df <- broom::tidy(summary)

TukeyHSD(summary)

tukey_df <- broom::tidy(TukeyHSD(summary))


wb <- createWorkbook()
addWorksheet(wb, "ANOVA")
addWorksheet(wb, "TukeyHSD")
writeData(wb, "ANOVA", anova_df)
writeData(wb, "TukeyHSD", tukey_df)
saveWorkbook(wb, "Data/Claude/analysis_non_college_deeper/High school accomplishments/MCA-M.xlsx", overwrite = TRUE)
```

### `MCA.R`

MCA Reading scores are significantly associated with disconnection at the omnibus level (F=6.7, p\<.001), but the Tukey contrasts reveal a more nuanced picture. The only pairwise differences that reach significance are between the persistently disconnected group and both the intermittently disconnected (estimate=−0.055, p=.001) and broadly disconnected groups (estimate=−0.063, p=.005). Consistently attached students do not differ significantly from any other group in pairwise comparisons. This suggests that reading proficiency primarily distinguishes the persistently disconnected from other non-completers, rather than mapping cleanly onto the full disconnection spectrum as math scores do.

```{r}
summary <- aov(MCA.R ~ disconnected.cat, data = master)

summary

anova_df <- broom::tidy(summary)

TukeyHSD(summary)

tukey_df <- broom::tidy(TukeyHSD(summary))

wb <- createWorkbook()
addWorksheet(wb, "ANOVA")
addWorksheet(wb, "TukeyHSD")
writeData(wb, "ANOVA", anova_df)
writeData(wb, "TukeyHSD", tukey_df)
saveWorkbook(wb, "Data/Claude/analysis_non_college_deeper/High school accomplishments/MCA-R.xlsx", overwrite = TRUE)
```

### `MCA.S`

MCA Science scores do not reach statistical significance across disconnection categories at the omnibus level (F=2.2, p=.091), and no individual Tukey contrast approaches significance — the closest being persistently vs. consistently attached (estimate=−0.041, p=.079). Science assessments in Minnesota were administered at fewer grade levels, and the smaller analytic sample (residual df \~22,539 vs. \~30,000 for math and reading) reduces statistical power. Substantively, science performance appears to be the weakest academic signal for distinguishing labor market attachment trajectories among non-completers in this population.

```{r}
summary <- aov(MCA.S ~ disconnected.cat, data = master)

summary

anova_df <- broom::tidy(summary)

TukeyHSD(summary)

tukey_df <- broom::tidy(TukeyHSD(summary))

wb <- createWorkbook()
```

### `cte.achievement`

CTE achievement level is the strongest predictor among all high school accomplishment variables (χ²=635.3, df=6, p\<.001, Cramer's V=0.098). A clear protective gradient emerges: CTE Concentrators/Completors have the lowest persistent disconnection rate (40.9%), followed by CTE Participants (45.5%), with those who had no CTE involvement showing the highest rate (56.1%). The consistently attached rate follows the inverse pattern: 20% for Concentrators/Completors, 15.3% for Participants, and only 11.4% for No CTE. This is the most practically actionable finding in this variable set — deeper CTE engagement is associated with meaningfully better post-school labor market outcomes for non-completers.

```{r}
tab_xtab(var.row = master$disconnected.cat, var.col = master$cte.achievement, 
         title = "", 
         show.exp = TRUE,

         file = "Data/Claude/analysis_non_college_deeper/High school accomplishments/cte-achievement.html")
```

### `total.cte.courses.taken`

Total CTE courses taken is the strongest continuous predictor in the high school accomplishments domain (F=246.0, p\<.001), and uniquely, every pairwise Tukey contrast is statistically significant. Persistently disconnected students took approximately 1.31 fewer CTE courses than consistently attached peers (estimate=−1.314, p\<.001), and the gradient holds across all group comparisons — including broadly vs. intermittently disconnected (estimate=−0.321, p\<.001) and persistently vs. broadly disconnected (estimate=−0.553, p\<.001). Unlike the academic score variables, CTE course-taking differentiates all four disconnection categories from one another, suggesting a dose-response relationship between CTE exposure and labor market attachment that operates across the full spectrum of disconnection.

```{r}

summary

anova_df <- broom::tidy(summary)

TukeyHSD(summary)
```

## Post-secondary

- Post-secondary
  - `attended.ps`

### Summary

Postsecondary attendance is the single strongest predictor of disconnection outcomes in the entire analysis (χ²=1094.7, df=3, p\<.001, Cramer's V=0.182). The relationship is substantial and runs in both directions. Among those who never attended postsecondary, 53.1% were persistently disconnected and only 12.4% were consistently attached. Among those who did attend — but did not complete, by definition of this sample — persistent disconnection drops to 36.5% and consistent attachment rises to 22.0%. The \~17-point gap in persistent disconnection between attenders and non-attenders is the largest single split observed across any binary variable in the analysis.

Notably, postsecondary attendance also elevates intermittent disconnection (30.1% vs. 22.6%), which likely reflects the transitional disruption of enrollment and exit — students who attended but left may cycle in and out of the labor market more actively than those who never attempted postsecondary at all. The broadly disconnected category is nearly identical across attendance groups (11.4% vs. 11.9%), suggesting that mid-range disconnection is not strongly tied to postsecondary experience.

For non-completers, postsecondary attendance — even without a credential — is associated with meaningfully better labor market attachment. This may reflect human capital gains from partial enrollment, stronger job-search networks, or selection of more labor-market-oriented individuals into attempted enrollment. The finding also reinforces the AP exam and PSEO paradox noted in the high school accomplishments domain: college-oriented pathways improve outcomes on average, but the non-completers who traveled furthest down those pathways without finishing are not among the most protected.

## OVERALL SUMMARY — BIVARIATE ANALYSIS OF DISCONNECTION PERSISTENCE Non-College Completers, Southeast Minnesota (EDR 9 and 10) 2008–2018 High School Graduate Cohorts \| n=32,878

**OVERVIEW**

The bivariate analysis of disconnection persistence among non-college completers examines four variable domains: demographic characteristics, high school context, high school accomplishments, and postsecondary orientation. Across 21 variables, a consistent and coherent picture emerges. Chronic labor market detachment — persistent disconnection across 4 or more of the first 5 years after exiting formal education — is the modal outcome for this population at 46.5%. It is not, however, uniformly distributed. The variables that most powerfully differentiate persistent disconnection from consistent attachment are postsecondary attendance, CTE engagement, and specific demographic characteristics. Place-based high school context variables show negligible associations throughout.

**DOMAIN 1: HIGH SCHOOL CONTEXT (Negligible associations)**

The four high school context variables — EDR, community type (Dem_Desc), average local unemployment rate, and average local wages as a percent of the state average — show no meaningful association with disconnection persistence. EDR (V=0.021) and Dem_Desc (V=0.014) reach statistical significance only due to sample size, with persistent disconnection rates varying by less than 2 percentage points across categories. Both continuous economic context variables (unemployment rate, wage level) are marginally significant at the omnibus level but show no meaningful pairwise differentiation between consistently attached and persistently disconnected graduates. Where a non-college completer attended high school within Southeast Minnesota has essentially no bearing on whether they experience chronic labor market detachment. Place-based factors are consistently the weakest domain in this analysis.

**DOMAIN 2: DEMOGRAPHIC CHARACTERISTICS (Modest to meaningful associations)**

Demographic variables show consistent and meaningful associations with disconnection persistence, confirming that chronic labor market detachment is not randomly distributed across the population. Every demographic disadvantage examined is associated with higher persistent disconnection and lower consistent attachment — the variation is in magnitude, not direction.

Special education status is the strongest demographic predictor (V=0.113). More than one in two special education non-completers is persistently disconnected (56.9%), compared to 43.6% for non-special education graduates — a 13.3 percentage point gap that is the largest binary demographic differential in the analysis. English learner status is the second strongest (V=0.096), with 59.9% persistent disconnection — the highest absolute rate of any binary demographic variable — reflecting a chronic detachment signature rather than cyclical unemployment.

Race and ethnicity shows a moderate association (V=0.060), with substantial variation across groups. White graduates show the lowest persistent disconnection (44.8%). Black graduates (62.8%) and American Indian graduates (66.0%) show the highest rates — gaps of more than 20 percentage points relative to White graduates. These are among the most analytically striking findings in the demographic domain. Gender (V=0.073) and economic status (V=0.070) show similar magnitudes, each producing roughly 4–5 percentage point persistent disconnection gaps, with males and low-income graduates disadvantaged. The language minority variables (non.english.home, LimitedEnglishProficiencyIndicator) add limited independent value beyond english.learner but confirm the chronic disconnection pattern for language minority non-completers.

Demographic disadvantages are not mutually exclusive. Graduates facing multiple simultaneous disadvantages — for example, Black or American Indian graduates who are also economically disadvantaged and lack CTE engagement — face compounded disconnection risks that single-variable analyses cannot fully capture.

**DOMAIN 3: HIGH SCHOOL ACCOMPLISHMENTS (Small to moderate associations)**

The high school accomplishments domain confirms that CTE engagement is the most consequential in-school predictor of labor market attachment among non-completers — more so than any academic achievement measure.

CTE achievement level is the strongest variable in the domain (V=0.098). CTE Concentrators and Completors show 40.9% persistent disconnection — the lowest of any accomplishments subgroup — compared to 56.1% for those with no CTE involvement, a gap of more than 15 percentage points. Total CTE courses taken reinforces this finding with the largest F-statistic of any continuous variable (F=246.0) and the unique distinction of every pairwise Tukey contrast reaching significance, indicating a true dose-response relationship across the full disconnection spectrum.

Academic achievement measures show consistent but smaller associations. ACT composite score produces the largest academic effect (F=70.6), with persistently disconnected students scoring approximately 1.4 points below consistently attached peers. ACT participation itself is also protective, with a 7-point persistent disconnection gap between test-takers and non-takers. MCA Math shows a consistent negative gradient (F=19.9) concentrated between the persistently disconnected group and all others. MCA Reading reaches omnibus significance (F=6.7) but only meaningfully distinguishes the persistently disconnected from the middle two categories. MCA Science is non-significant at both the omnibus and pairwise levels — the only academic measure to fail entirely.

The college-access variables (AP exam, PSEO) present an important interpretive caution. AP exam participation is associated with paradoxically higher persistent disconnection (51.9% vs. 46.5% overall), and PSEO participation is a null predictor (p=.067). For non-completers, these markers likely reflect interrupted college trajectories rather than workforce readiness — students who signaled college intent in high school but did not sustain enrollment, and who subsequently experienced greater, not lesser, labor market difficulty.

**DOMAIN 4: POSTSECONDARY ORIENTATION (Strongest association in the analysis)**

Postsecondary attendance is the single strongest predictor of disconnection outcomes across all four domains (V=0.182). Among those who never attended postsecondary, 53.1% were persistently disconnected and only 12.4% were consistently attached. Among those who attended but did not complete, persistent disconnection drops to 36.5% and consistent attachment rises to 22.0% — a \~17 percentage point gap in persistent disconnection that is the largest single split observed for any binary variable in the analysis. Even without a credential, postsecondary attendance is associated with meaningfully better labor market attachment, likely reflecting human capital gains from partial enrollment, stronger employment networks, or positive selection of more labor-market-oriented individuals into attempted enrollment.

**SYNTHESIS**

Three cross-cutting conclusions organize the findings.

First, chronic disconnection is structured, not random. The persistence framework reveals durable stratification that point-in-time analyses understate. Special education graduates, English learners, Black and American Indian graduates, and those with no CTE or postsecondary exposure face systematically higher rates of chronic labor market detachment that accumulate across the five-year window and do not resolve on their own.

Second, the most actionable protective factors are CTE engagement and postsecondary attendance, in that order of what can be influenced through high school policy. CTE depth — measured both as achievement level and course volume — is the strongest in-school predictor and operates as a genuine dose-response gradient. Even partial postsecondary attendance without completion substantially reduces persistent disconnection, pointing to the value of supported transitions to postsecondary even when completion is not guaranteed.

Third, college-preparatory signaling in high school (AP exams, PSEO) does not function as a protective factor for non-completers and may modestly compound disadvantage. For this population, the more relevant preparation pathway runs through applied and technical education, not college-orientation markers.

Place-based characteristics — where in Southeast Minnesota a graduate attended high school — are consistently and decisively the least important predictors of disconnection persistence. Individual-level characteristics, particularly CTE engagement, demographic disadvantage, and postsecondary experience, account for the meaningful variation in chronic labor market detachment among non-college completers.

<br>

# Relationship Between Individual Characteristics and the year-to-year refined disconnection categories

This analysis is focused on whether any variables that are most likely to show up in each of these categories. With such small numbers of individuals among the more refined workforce state categories, let's combine some of them before the analysis. So let's collapse into three primary categories;

1.  Group A: No MN employment record
2.  Group B: In-Region Marginal Employment
    1.  This group will be only the `Not meaningful_in_only` and is our local underutilization group.
3.  Group C: Other Disconnected Employment
    1.  This group contains all other `Not meaningful` employment categories.
        1.  `Not meaningful_out_only`
        2.  `Not meaningful_unclassified_only`
        3.  `Not meaningful_mixed_in_out_simultaneous`
        4.  `Not meaningful_mixed_in_unclassified_simultaneous`
        5.  `Not meaningful_mixed_out_unclassified_simultaneous`
        6.  `Not meaningful_mixed_in_out_unclassified_simultaneous`
        7.  `Not meaningful_mixed_in_out_sequential`
        8.  `Not meaningful_mixed_in_unclassified_sequential`
        9.  `Not meaningful_mixed_out_unclassified_sequential`
        10. `Not meaningful_mixed_in_out_unclassified_sequential`

I will also be including the "Sustained WF - Region" and "Sustained WF - MN" as seperate categories as well.

And just like before, we are going to measure the relationships between independent variables and the workforce participation categories for each after.ed.x. Here are the variables again;

- Demographics
  - `Gender`
  - `EconomicStatus`
  - `SpecialEdStatus`
  - `RaceEthnicity`
  - `english.learner`
  - `non.english.home`
  - `LimitedEnglishProficiencyIndicator`
- High school characteristics
  - `Dem_Desc`
  - `edr`
  - `avg.unemp.rate`
  - `avg.wages.pct.state`
- High school academics
  - `pseo.participant`
  - `took.ACT`
  - `ACTCompositeScore`
  - `ap.exam`
  - `MCA.M`
  - `MCA.R`
  - `MCA.S`
  - `cte.achievement`
  - `total.cte.courses.taken`
- Post-secondary
  - `attended.ps`

First we will collapse the workforce participation categories into the three groups.

```{r}
new.groups <- master %>%
  select(PersonID, after.ed.1:after.ed.5) %>%
  pivot_longer(names_to = "after.ed", values_to = "wf.state", after.ed.1:after.ed.5) %>%
  mutate(new.wf.state = ifelse(wf.state %in% c("Non-sustained WF_out_only", "Non-sustained WF_unclassified_only", "Non-sustained WF_mixed_in_out_simultaneous", "Non-sustained WF_mixed_in_unclassified_simultaneous", "Non-sustained WF_mixed_out_unclassified_simultaneous", "Non-sustained WF_mixed_in_out_unclassified_simultaneous", "Non-sustained WF_mixed_in_out_sequential", "Non-sustained WF_mixed_in_unclassified_sequential", "Non-sustained WF_mixed_out_unclassified_sequential", "Non-sustained WF_mixed_in_out_unclassified_sequential"), "Non-sustained WF - other", wf.state),
         new.wf.state = fct_relevel(new.wf.state, "Sustained WF - Region", "Sustained WF - MN", "Non-sustained WF_in_only", "Non-sustained WF - other", "No MN employment record")) %>%
  select(PersonID, after.ed, new.wf.state) %>%
  pivot_wider(names_from = after.ed, values_from = new.wf.state)

data.analysis <- master %>%
  select(-after.ed.1:-after.ed.5) %>%
  left_join(new.groups, by = "PersonID")

kable(head(data.analysis))  

kable(names(data.analysis))

```

## Demographics

Here are the independent variables we are exploring;

- Demographics
  - `Gender`

  - `EconomicStatus`

  - `SpecialEdStatus`

  - `RaceEthnicity`

  - `english.learner`

  - `non.english.home`

  - `LimitedEnglishProficiencyIndicator`

### Summary

**OVERVIEW**

The demographic variables collectively reveal that refined workforce participation outcomes among non-college completers are strongly and consistently stratified by individual characteristics across the full five-year observation window. Every demographic disadvantage examined is associated with lower sustained regional employment and higher concentration in the no MN employment record category. The variation across variables is in the magnitude, location, and trajectory of disadvantage — not its direction. Three cross-cutting patterns organize the findings.

**PATTERN 1: TWO DISTINCT DISADVANTAGE SIGNATURES**

The demographic variables divide into two analytically distinct disadvantage signatures based on where non-completers are concentrated when they are not in sustained employment.

The geographic absence signature is the defining characteristic of language minority non-completers (english.learner, non.english.home, LEP) and most racial and ethnic minority groups. These graduates are massively overrepresented in the no MN employment record category — more than four in ten English learner, non-English-home, and LEP non-completers have no Minnesota employment record by Year 5. They are simultaneously underrepresented in in-region marginal employment, meaning they do not show up in local underutilization counts. Their disadvantage is best characterized as labor market absence rather than local underutilization.

The local underutilization signature is more characteristic of special education graduates and, to a lesser degree, low-income and female non-completers. These groups are overrepresented in in-region marginal employment — present and employed in the region but not achieving sustained attachment. Special education graduates additionally show a persistent and large no-record concentration (\~33% at every year), combining both signatures simultaneously. Economic status produces a pure local underutilization pattern, with no-record rates that are virtually identical across income groups throughout all five years.

**PATTERN 2: VARIABLE TRAJECTORIES OVER TIME**

The five-year trajectories differ meaningfully across demographic variables, with three distinct patterns.

Accumulating disadvantage: Economic status shows a growing effect size (V=0.049 to V=0.084) as low-income non-completers fall further behind in sustained employment and become more concentrated in both non-sustained categories over time. The disadvantage compounds rather than resolves.

Stable disadvantage: Special education status (V≈0.098–0.109), english.learner (V≈0.093–0.103), and non.english.home (V≈0.095–0.107) show largely stable associations across the five years — the disadvantage is established at labor market entry and does not meaningfully narrow or widen. These groups face a structural disadvantage that the five-year window does not resolve.

Attenuating disadvantage: Gender shows a declining effect size (V=0.078 to V=0.063), with the male advantage in sustained regional employment and female overrepresentation in non-sustained categories both narrowing modestly over time.

**PATTERN 3: RANKING BY STRENGTH OF ASSOCIATION**

Across the five years, the ranking of demographic variables by effect size is consistent. Special education status and the language minority variables (english.learner, non.english.home) are the strongest predictors. Race and ethnicity shows a moderate but distinctive association driven by the Black no-record trajectory and Black other- disconnected employment overrepresentation — patterns not fully captured by a single Cramer's V. Gender and economic status are meaningful but smaller in magnitude. LEP is confirmatory of the language minority pattern but limited by small group size.

**POLICY IMPLICATIONS**

The two-signature finding has direct implications for intervention design. Local workforce programs targeting underutilization — in-region marginal employment — will primarily reach special education graduates, low-income non-completers, and female non-completers. Language minority non-completers and most racial and ethnic minority groups are largely absent from the measurable Minnesota labor market and will not be reached by programs that rely on labor market contact as a point of entry. Outreach strategies that do not depend on employment record identification are needed to reach the geographic absence population.

<br>

### `Gender`

OVERVIEW AND EFFECT SIZE

Gender shows a consistent, statistically significant but small association with refined workforce participation outcomes across all five years (V=0.078, 0.069, 0.067, 0.072, 0.063 at Years 1–5 respectively). The association is strongest in Year 1 and gradually attenuates, though it remains significant throughout. The direction and character of the gender differences are stable across the five-year window — this is not a relationship that fundamentally changes shape over time, but one that modestly weakens as the population sorts into more stable long-term states.

SUSTAINED WF — REGION

Males are consistently overrepresented in sustained regional employment across all five years. At Year 1, 26.8% of males are in Sustained WF — Region compared to 22.1% of females — a 4.7 percentage point gap. This gap widens modestly through Year 3 (31.4% vs. 26.9%, a 4.5 point gap) and persists through Year 5 (32.4% vs. 28.0%, a 4.4 point gap). The male advantage in regional sustained employment is present from the first year and remains structurally stable. This likely reflects the concentration of male non-completers in trade, construction, and manufacturing occupations that offer immediate full-time regional employment without credential requirements.

SUSTAINED WF — MN (OUT OF REGION)

Gender differences in out-of-region sustained employment are negligible across all five years. At Year 1 the gap is 0.3 percentage points (10.0% female vs. 9.7% male), and it never exceeds 1 percentage point in any year. By Year 5 females show 14.8% and males 15.7% in this category. This is a consistent null finding — gender does not differentiate who leaves the region for sustained employment elsewhere in Minnesota.

IN-REGION MARGINAL EMPLOYMENT (Non-sustained WF_in_only)

Females are overrepresented in in-region marginal employment across all five years. At Year 1, 20.8% of females are in this category compared to 19.3% of males. The female overrepresentation grows modestly and stabilizes: by Year 4 the gap is 2.5 percentage points (13.7% vs. 11.2%) and at Year 5 it is 1.4 percentage points (11.9% vs. 10.5%). Both groups show declining rates in this category over time as the population shifts toward sustained employment or no MN record, but females consistently show higher in-region marginal employment rates. This is the local underutilization signature for female non-completers — present and employed in the region, but not achieving sustained attachment.

OTHER DISCONNECTED EMPLOYMENT (Non-sustained WF — other)

Females are notably overrepresented in other disconnected employment throughout the five-year window, and this is the category where the gender gap is most pronounced. At Year 1, 22.5% of females are in this category compared to 17.5% of males — a 5.0 percentage point gap that is the largest single-category gender differential in Year 1. The gap narrows but persists: Year 3 (17.4% vs. 13.9%, 3.5 points), Year 5 (14.3% vs. 11.2%, 3.1 points). Combined with the in-region marginal employment finding, female non-completers are substantially more concentrated across both non-sustained employment categories than males at every time point.

NO MN EMPLOYMENT RECORD

Males are modestly overrepresented in the no MN employment record category at Year 1 (26.7% vs. 24.6%), a 2.1 percentage point gap. This gap narrows rapidly and is essentially eliminated by Year 3 (29.2% vs. 28.5%) and Year 4 (29.6% vs. 29.4%). By Year 5 the distributions are nearly identical (30.3% male vs. 31.0% female), with females marginally exceeding males. The early male overrepresentation likely reflects a subset of male non-completers who leave Minnesota immediately — possibly for military service, out-of-state employment, or seasonal work — before establishing a Minnesota employment record. The convergence by Year 3 suggests these males either return to Minnesota employment or the female no-record rate catches up as some female non-completers exhaust non-sustained employment options.

TRAJECTORY SUMMARY

The overall five-year trajectory for both groups follows the same directional pattern: declining shares in both non-sustained employment categories and growing shares in sustained regional employment and no MN employment record. Gender does not change the direction of these trends but consistently positions females with lower sustained regional employment and higher non-sustained (particularly other disconnected) employment at every time point. The male advantage in Sustained WF — Region is the most durable and policy-relevant gender finding across the five years, while the female concentration in both non-sustained categories — particularly other disconnected employment — represents the clearest gender-differentiated workforce disadvantage in this population.

### `economic.status`

OVERVIEW AND EFFECT SIZE

Economic status shows a consistent, statistically significant, and gradually strengthening association with refined workforce participation outcomes across all five years (V=0.049, 0.056, 0.061, 0.065, 0.084 at Years 1–5 respectively). This trajectory is notably different from gender, where the association attenuated over time. Here the association grows stronger as the observation window extends, suggesting that economic disadvantage does not simply delay workforce attachment — it compounds it. The Year 5 effect size (V=0.084) is the largest in the sequence and exceeds the Year 1 value by nearly double, making economic status one of the more temporally dynamic variables in this analysis.

SUSTAINED WF — REGION

Non-low-income graduates (coded 0) consistently show higher sustained regional employment rates across all five years. At Year 1 the gap is 2.5 percentage points (25.9% vs. 23.4%). This gap widens steadily: Year 3 (31.0% vs. 27.4%, 3.6 points), Year 4 (31.5% vs. 28.4%, 3.1 points), Year 5 (32.2% vs. 28.2%, 4.0 points). The non-low-income advantage in sustained regional employment is present from the outset and persists without narrowing across the five-year window. Economic disadvantage consistently depresses the probability of achieving sustained regional employment, and this disadvantage does not close over time.

SUSTAINED WF — MN (OUT OF REGION)

Non-low-income graduates show modestly higher out-of-region sustained employment across all years. At Year 1 the gap is 0.7 percentage points (10.1% vs. 9.4%), widening to 2.6 points by Year 5 (16.4% vs. 13.8%). Like regional sustained employment, the out-of-region gap grows rather than narrows over time. The pattern suggests that non-low-income non-completers have somewhat greater access to sustained employment opportunities anywhere in Minnesota, not just within the region.

IN-REGION MARGINAL EMPLOYMENT (Non-sustained WF_in_only)

At Year 1, in-region marginal employment rates are essentially identical across economic status groups (19.9% vs. 19.8%) — a genuine null finding at the starting point. The gap emerges and grows over time, but in the direction of greater low-income overrepresentation: Year 2 (16.7% vs. 15.7%, 1.0 point), Year 3 (14.7% vs. 12.8%, 1.9 points), Year 4 (13.7% vs. 11.2%, 2.5 points), Year 5 (12.8% vs. 9.8%, 3.0 points). This trajectory is analytically important: low-income non-completers do not start out more concentrated in local marginal employment, but they become increasingly concentrated there relative to non-low-income peers as time passes. This is a local underutilization pattern that accumulates — low- income graduates who remain in the region but fail to achieve sustained attachment are not exiting this category at the same rate as non-low- income graduates.

OTHER DISCONNECTED EMPLOYMENT (Non-sustained WF — other)

Low-income graduates are overrepresented in other disconnected employment at every time point, and this is the category with the largest economic status gap at Year 1. At Year 1, 21.7% of low-income graduates are in this category compared to 18.0% of non-low-income graduates — a 3.7 percentage point gap. The gap narrows over time as overall rates in this category decline: Year 3 (17.2% vs. 14.0%, 3.2 points), Year 5 (14.6% vs. 10.9%, 3.7 points). The gap at Year 5 is essentially unchanged from Year 1 in absolute terms, meaning that low-income graduates are not exiting other disconnected employment into sustained employment at the same rate as non-low-income graduates. Combined with the in-region marginal employment finding, low-income non-completers are more concentrated across both non-sustained categories at every time point and the gap in other disconnected employment does not close over time.

NO MN EMPLOYMENT RECORD

No MN employment record rates are nearly identical across economic status groups at every time point. At Year 1 the gap is just 0.5 percentage points (26.1% vs. 25.6%), and it remains within 1 percentage point through Year 4 (29.6% vs. 29.4%). By Year 5 the distributions are virtually identical (30.6% vs. 30.5%). This is a consistent null finding across all five years. Economic disadvantage does not meaningfully differentiate who has no Minnesota employment record — low-income and non-low-income non-completers leave or remain absent from Minnesota employment at essentially the same rate. This distinguishes economic status from variables like english.learner and race/ethnicity, where no-record rates show larger differentials reflecting geographic departure or absence signatures.

TRAJECTORY SUMMARY

The economic status story across five years is one of accumulating disadvantage concentrated in the two non-sustained employment categories rather than geographic departure. Low-income non-completers are not more likely to have no Minnesota employment record — they are more likely to be employed in the region or elsewhere in Minnesota but without achieving sustained attachment. This local underutilization signature strengthens over time, particularly in in-region marginal employment, where the gap grows from essentially zero at Year 1 to 3.0 percentage points by Year 5. The growing effect size (V=0.049 to V=0.084) reflects this accumulation dynamic: economic disadvantage becomes a more powerful differentiator of workforce outcomes as the observation window extends, not less. This pattern is meaningfully different from gender, where the association attenuated, and points to economic status as a variable whose workforce consequences deepen with time among non-completers who remain in the Minnesota labor market.

### `SpecialEdStatus`

OVERVIEW AND EFFECT SIZE

Special education status shows the strongest and most stable association with refined workforce participation outcomes of any binary demographic variable across all five years (V=0.109, 0.101, 0.098, 0.091, 0.098 at Years 1–5). The association is strongest in Year 1, dips modestly through Year 4, then partially recovers at Year 5. Unlike economic status, which grew stronger over time, the special education association is largest at the point of labor market entry — reflecting an immediate and severe disadvantage that is present from the first year.

SUSTAINED WF — REGION

Non-special education graduates show substantially higher sustained regional employment at every time point. At Year 1 the gap is 6.3 percentage points (26.3% vs. 20.0%). This gap widens and stabilizes: Year 3 (30.8% vs. 24.9%, 5.9 points), Year 5 (31.6% vs. 26.7%, 4.9 points). The gap narrows somewhat by Year 5 but remains meaningful throughout. Special education non-completers are consistently less likely to achieve sustained regional employment at every observation point across the five-year window.

SUSTAINED WF — MN (OUT OF REGION)

The out-of-region sustained employment gap is large and grows over time. At Year 1 it is 4.2 percentage points (10.7% vs. 6.5%). By Year 5 it reaches 5.9 percentage points (16.6% vs. 10.7%). Special education non-completers are consistently less likely to achieve sustained employment anywhere in Minnesota, and this disadvantage deepens as the window extends. This is the category where the special education gap grows most sharply over time, suggesting that non-special education graduates who do not achieve regional sustained employment are more likely to find sustained employment elsewhere in the state — an option that appears less available to special education non-completers.

IN-REGION MARGINAL EMPLOYMENT (Non-sustained WF_in_only)

Special education graduates are overrepresented in in-region marginal employment at every time point — the reverse of the sustained employment pattern. At Year 1: 22.3% vs. 19.2%, a 3.1 point gap. The gap holds through Year 3 (16.5% vs. 12.8%, 3.7 points) and Year 5 (13.8% vs. 10.3%, 3.5 points). Special education non-completers who remain in Minnesota employment are disproportionately concentrated in local marginal employment — employed in the region but not achieving sustained attachment — at every time point. This local underutilization signature is stable and does not narrow over the five years.

OTHER DISCONNECTED EMPLOYMENT (Non-sustained WF — other)

Special education and non-special education graduates show nearly identical other disconnected employment rates at most time points. At Year 1: 18.6% vs. 19.9% — special education graduates are actually slightly underrepresented. At Year 5: 15.2% vs. 11.7%, a 3.5 point gap emerges with special education graduates overrepresented. This category shows the most muted and delayed economic status differentiation of any outcome category, suggesting that other disconnected employment does not strongly select on special education status in early years but does by Year 5.

NO MN EMPLOYMENT RECORD

Special education graduates are substantially overrepresented in the no MN employment record category at every time point, and this is the most distinctive feature of their workforce participation profile. At Year 1: 32.7% vs. 23.9% — a 8.8 percentage point gap that is the largest single-category, single-year differential for any binary variable in the demographic group. This gap is remarkably stable: Year 2 (32.7% vs. 25.6%), Year 3 (33.8% vs. 27.5%), Year 4 (33.6% vs. 28.4%), Year 5 (33.5% vs. 29.7%). One in three special education non-completers has no Minnesota employment record at every observation point. This persistent no-record signature suggests a substantial subgroup of special education non-completers who do not establish meaningful labor market contact in the region or elsewhere in Minnesota across the entire five-year window.

### `RaceEthnicity`

INTERPRETIVE NOTE: American Indian graduates (n=212) represent a very small group. Percentage estimates for this group are unstable and should be interpreted with caution throughout.

OVERVIEW AND EFFECT SIZE

Race and ethnicity shows a consistent, moderate association with refined workforce participation outcomes across all five years (V=0.060, 0.060, 0.059, 0.059, 0.064 at Years 1–5). The effect size is remarkably stable — essentially flat from Year 1 through Year 4 before a slight uptick at Year 5 (V=0.064). The overall association is driven primarily by the no MN employment record category, where minority groups — particularly American Indian and Asian/PI graduates — are substantially overrepresented relative to White graduates, and by the other disconnected employment category, where Black graduates show a distinctive and persistent overrepresentation.

SUSTAINED WF — REGION

White graduates show the highest sustained regional employment rates at every time point. At Year 1: 26.1%, growing to 32.2% by Year 5. Hispanic graduates are the closest to White graduates (22.8% at Year 1, 26.1% by Year 5). Black graduates show substantially lower sustained regional employment (13.1% at Year 1, 15.3% by Year 5) — a persistent gap of roughly 13 percentage points relative to White graduates that does not close over the five-year window. Asian/PI graduates show 19.5% at Year 1 rising to 23.0% by Year 5 — below White graduates but above Black graduates. American Indian estimates are highly variable given small n.

SUSTAINED WF — MN (OUT OF REGION)

Out-of-region sustained employment rates are broadly similar across groups, with differences smaller than in the regional category. At Year 5, rates range from 12.3% (American Indian, interpret with caution) to 15.8% (Hispanic) and 15.6% (Asian/PI), with White graduates at 15.4% and Black graduates at 13.7%. The out-of-region category does not show the same strong racial stratification as sustained regional employment, suggesting that when minority non-completers do achieve sustained employment, they are not dramatically less likely to find it elsewhere in Minnesota.

IN-REGION MARGINAL EMPLOYMENT (Non-sustained WF_in_only)

White graduates are consistently overrepresented in in-region marginal employment relative to all minority groups. At Year 1, White graduates show 20.8% in this category compared to 15.7% for Black, 15.5% for Asian/PI, and 14.9% for Hispanic graduates. This pattern persists through Year 5 (11.4% White vs. 9.8% Hispanic, 9.1% Asian/PI, 8.7% Black). This is a counterintuitive finding — White non-completers are more likely to be employed locally but not at sustained levels. This likely reflects White graduates' greater access to local part-time, seasonal, or intermittent employment in the regional economy, while minority non-completers are more likely to be entirely absent from the Minnesota employment record.

OTHER DISCONNECTED EMPLOYMENT (Non-sustained WF — other)

Black graduates show a strikingly distinctive profile in other disconnected employment across all five years. At Year 1, 32.3% of Black non-completers are in this category — nearly double the White rate of 18.8% and far above any other group. This elevated rate persists: Year 3 (26.7% vs. 14.5% White), Year 5 (24.1% vs. 11.7% White). The Black non-completer other disconnected employment rate is the largest and most persistent single- category differential across any demographic subgroup in the entire five- year analysis. This pattern suggests Black non-completers who do have Minnesota employment records are disproportionately concentrated in fragmented, multi-location, or otherwise non-sustained employment patterns that do not resolve over time.

NO MN EMPLOYMENT RECORD

All minority groups show higher no MN employment record rates than White graduates across the full five-year window. At Year 1: American Indian 42.5%, Asian/PI 36.4%, Hispanic 31.7%, Black 28.6%, White 24.7%. These gaps widen slightly over time. By Year 5: American Indian 44.3%, Asian/PI 40.6%, Hispanic 35.6%, Black 38.3%, White 29.2%. The increasing no-record rates for Black graduates (28.6% to 38.3%) and the persistently high rates for American Indian and Asian/PI graduates reflect a geographic departure or absence signature — minority non-completers are increasingly likely to have no Minnesota employment record as the window extends, rather than transitioning into sustained employment as White graduates do.

### `english.learner`

OVERVIEW AND EFFECT SIZE

English learner status shows a strong and relatively stable association with refined workforce participation outcomes across all five years (V=0.103, 0.103, 0.093, 0.096, 0.098 at Years 1–5). The effect is strongest in Years 1–2, dips modestly at Year 3, and partially recovers through Year 5. This is one of the stronger demographic associations in the analysis, driven overwhelmingly by the no MN employment record category where English learners are massively overrepresented at every time point.

SUSTAINED WF — REGION

Non-English learner graduates show substantially higher sustained regional employment rates at every time point. At Year 1: 25.8% vs. 17.6% — an 8.2 percentage point gap. This gap narrows slightly but persists: Year 3 (30.6% vs. 20.9%), Year 5 (31.8% vs. 20.6%). The English learner sustained regional employment rate grows over time (17.6% to 20.6%) but never approaches the non-English learner rate. English learner non- completers face a persistent 10+ point deficit in sustained regional employment across the full five-year window.

SUSTAINED WF — MN (OUT OF REGION)

Out-of-region sustained employment rates are essentially equivalent across English learner status groups at every time point. At Year 1: 9.8% for both groups. By Year 5: 15.7% non-English learner vs. 12.7% English learner — a modest 3-point gap. This is a much smaller differential than the regional sustained employment gap, suggesting that when English learner non-completers do achieve sustained employment, they find it within and outside the region at roughly similar rates relative to non- English learners.

IN-REGION MARGINAL EMPLOYMENT (Non-sustained WF_in_only)

English learners show lower in-region marginal employment rates than non-English learners at most time points — a counterintuitive finding. At Year 1: 16.4% vs. 20.3%. By Year 5: 11.3% vs. 11.1% — essentially converged. The lower in-region marginal employment rate for English learners reflects their much higher no-record concentration: English learner non-completers who lack sustained employment are more likely to be entirely absent from Minnesota employment records than to appear in local marginal employment. They are not underutilized locally — they are largely absent from the measurable Minnesota labor market.

OTHER DISCONNECTED EMPLOYMENT (Non-sustained WF — other)

English learner and non-English learner graduates show similar other disconnected employment rates across all five years. At Year 1: 18.4% vs. 19.7% — English learners slightly underrepresented. At Year 5: 14.2% vs. 12.2% — a modest 2-point English learner overrepresentation. This category does not meaningfully differentiate English learner status across the five years, consistent with the finding that English learner non-completer disadvantage is concentrated in the no-record category rather than in the character of their Minnesota employment when present.

NO MN EMPLOYMENT RECORD

The no MN employment record differential is the defining feature of the English learner workforce participation profile and is the largest single- category gap of any binary variable in the demographic group. At Year 1: 37.9% of English learner non-completers have no Minnesota employment record compared to 24.4% of non-English learners — a 13.5 percentage point gap. This gap grows and remains large across all five years: Year 2 (39.2% vs. 25.6%), Year 3 (39.7% vs. 27.5%), Year 4 (40.2% vs. 28.2%), Year 5 (41.2% vs. 29.2%). More than four in ten English learner non- completers have no Minnesota employment record by Year 5 — a rate that grows, not shrinks, over time. This is the clearest geographic departure or absence signature in the entire demographic variable group.

### `non.english.home`

OVERVIEW AND EFFECT SIZE

Non-English home language shows a strong association with refined workforce participation outcomes, strongest in Years 1–2 and stabilizing thereafter (V=0.107, 0.105, 0.095, 0.097, 0.096 at Years 1–5). The pattern closely parallels english.learner in magnitude and direction, which is expected given the conceptual overlap between the two variables. The main finding is the same: non-English home language non-completers are dramatically overrepresented in the no MN employment record category and underrepresented in sustained regional employment throughout the five-year window.

SUSTAINED WF — REGION

English-home graduates consistently show higher sustained regional employment. At Year 1: 25.6% vs. 18.7% — a 6.9 point gap. This gap holds through Year 5 (31.6% vs. 21.1%, 10.5 points). The gap widens over time as English-home graduates continue transitioning into sustained regional employment at a faster rate than non-English-home graduates.

SUSTAINED WF — MN (OUT OF REGION)

Unlike sustained regional employment, out-of-region sustained employment shows minimal differentiation by home language. At Year 1: 9.6% English- home vs. 11.1% non-English-home — non-English-home graduates are slightly overrepresented. This reverses by Year 3 (12.8% vs. 12.2%) and Year 5 (15.4% vs. 14.7%) with near-equivalent rates. The out-of-region category is essentially a null finding for home language, consistent with the english.learner pattern.

IN-REGION MARGINAL EMPLOYMENT (Non-sustained WF_in_only)

Non-English-home graduates show substantially lower in-region marginal employment than English-home graduates at every time point — the most pronounced reversal in this category across any demographic variable. At Year 1: 12.0% vs. 20.8% — an 8.8 percentage point gap with non- English-home graduates underrepresented. This gap narrows but persists: Year 3 (9.6% vs. 14.0%), Year 5 (8.1% vs. 11.4%). Non-English-home non-completers are consistently less likely to appear in local marginal employment, which is best interpreted alongside the no-record finding: this group is not showing up in local underutilization counts because they are largely absent from the Minnesota employment record, not because they are otherwise employed.

OTHER DISCONNECTED EMPLOYMENT (Non-sustained WF — other)

Other disconnected employment rates are similar across home language groups at most time points, with non-English-home graduates showing modest overrepresentation. At Year 1: 20.4% vs. 19.5%. At Year 5: 13.8% vs. 12.3%. The gap is small and consistent — other disconnected employment is not a primary differentiator of home language status.

NO MN EMPLOYMENT RECORD

The no MN employment record differential mirrors the english.learner pattern in magnitude. At Year 1: 37.8% of non-English-home graduates have no Minnesota employment record compared to 24.5% of English-home graduates — a 13.3 percentage point gap. This grows persistently: Year 3 (40.4% vs. 27.6%), Year 5 (42.3% vs. 29.3%). By Year 5, more than four in ten non-English-home non-completers have no Minnesota employment record. The non-English-home no-record rate exceeds even the english. learner rate by Year 5 (42.3% vs. 41.2%), suggesting that the broader language minority category captures some additional geographic absence not fully captured by formal English learner classification alone.

### `LimitedEnglishProficiencyIndicator`

INTERPRETIVE NOTE: The LEP group is small (n=803) relative to the non-LEP group (n=32,075). Percentage estimates for LEP graduates are less stable and should be interpreted with appropriate caution, particularly for individual outcome categories with small cell counts. An additional anomaly is present at Year 1, where LEP graduates show a higher Sustained WF — MN rate than non-LEP graduates (14.6% vs. 9.7%). Given the small LEP group size, this is likely a sampling artifact rather than a substantive finding and should not be over- interpreted. The pattern does not persist in subsequent years.

OVERVIEW AND EFFECT SIZE

LEP status shows a moderate and fluctuating association with refined workforce participation outcomes (V=0.060, 0.057, 0.048, 0.051, 0.055 at Years 1–5). The association is weakest at Year 3 and partially recovers through Year 5. Effect sizes are smaller than for english. learner or non.english.home, consistent with LEP being a narrower and more severe language classification applied to a smaller subgroup.

SUSTAINED WF — REGION

LEP graduates show lower sustained regional employment at every time point. At Year 1: 17.9% vs. 25.1% — a 7.2 point gap. By Year 5: 18.4% vs. 30.8% — a 12.4 point gap that grows over time. LEP graduates show essentially no improvement in sustained regional employment rates across the five years (17.9% to 18.4%), while non-LEP graduates improve substantially (25.1% to 30.8%). This is among the most striking trajectory differentials in the demographic group: LEP non-completers are not transitioning into sustained regional employment over time at any meaningful rate.

SUSTAINED WF — MN (OUT OF REGION)

As noted, Year 1 shows an anomalous LEP overrepresentation in out-of- region sustained employment (14.6% vs. 9.7%) that is likely a small-n artifact. By Year 3 the rates are nearly equivalent (11.8% vs. 12.7%) and by Year 5 LEP graduates show modestly lower rates (14.1% vs. 15.4%). This category should be interpreted cautiously for LEP graduates given group size.

IN-REGION MARGINAL EMPLOYMENT (Non-sustained WF_in_only)

LEP graduates show substantially lower in-region marginal employment than non-LEP graduates throughout — the same counterintuitive pattern seen for english.learner and non.english.home. At Year 1: 9.5% vs. 20.2%. By Year 5: 8.1% vs. 11.2%. LEP non-completers are not present in local marginal employment at meaningful rates, consistent with their high no-record concentration.

OTHER DISCONNECTED EMPLOYMENT (Non-sustained WF — other)

LEP graduates are modestly overrepresented in other disconnected employment at most time points. At Year 1: 21.3% vs. 19.5%. At Year 5: 15.6% vs. 12.4%. The gap is small and consistent, adding limited independent interpretive value beyond the no-record finding.

NO MN EMPLOYMENT RECORD

The no-record differential is the defining feature of the LEP profile and mirrors the english.learner and non.english.home patterns in direction, though with some variation due to small group size. At Year 1: 36.7% LEP vs. 25.6% non-LEP — an 11.1 point gap. This gap grows steadily: Year 3 (41.6% vs. 28.6%), Year 5 (43.8% vs. 30.2%). By Year 5, nearly 44% of LEP non-completers have no Minnesota employment record — the highest no-record rate of any language minority subgroup and among the highest of any demographic group in the analysis. As with english.learner and non.english.home, LEP non-completers are not transitioning out of no-record status over the five-year window. This variable is best treated as confirmatory of the language minority no-record signature rather than as an independent primary finding.

::: panel-tabset

## High School Characteristics

Here are the variables we are going to explore;

- `Dem_Desc`
- `edr`
- `avg.unemp.rate`
- `avg.wages.pct.state`

### Summary

**OVERVIEW**

The high school characteristics group confirms and extends the finding established throughout the disconnection persistence analysis: place- based factors have negligible independent associations with individual workforce outcomes, and this holds across the refined five-category outcome structure and across all five years of the observation window. Three of the four variables in this group are either non-significant for most or all years, or significant only due to sample size with trivially small practical effects. The one exception — average local unemployment rate — provides a substantively meaningful signal, but one that pertains to a contextual labor market push dynamic rather than individual-level outcome stratification.

**VARIABLE FINDINGS IN ORDER OF PRACTICAL SIGNIFICANCE**

Average local unemployment rate is the only high school characteristics variable with consistent and meaningful pairwise differentiation across the five years. Its primary contribution is not to differentiate good from bad outcomes broadly, but to identify a specific dynamic: graduates from higher-unemployment communities are more likely to achieve sustained employment outside the region (Sustained WF — MN) rather than within it. This contrast — between in-region employment of any kind (associated with lower local unemployment) and out-of- region sustained employment (associated with higher local unemployment) — is stable and significant from Year 2 onward. Local unemployment rate functions as a labor market push factor, not a uniform predictor of workforce disadvantage.

Community type (Dem_Desc) shows the only growing effect size in the group (V=0.030 to V=0.040), driven by a modest and accumulating advantage for entirely urban graduates in sustained regional employment and a modest overrepresentation of urban/town/rural mix graduates in the no-record category. Neither difference is large enough to warrant policy differentiation, but the gradual strengthening over time suggests that community type exerts a slow-accumulating influence on geographic labor market attachment — urban graduates root into the regional labor market at slightly higher rates, while graduates from more dispersed communities drift toward labor market absence.

EDR is a consistent null predictor at Years 1–2 and remains negligible through Year 5 (maximum V=0.034). Whether a non-completer attended high school in EDR 9 or EDR 10 has no bearing on their refined workforce participation trajectory at any point.

Average wages as a percent of state average is a complete null at Years 1–4, reaching marginal significance only at Year 5 with differences too small to interpret meaningfully. This variable adds no analytical value in any year.

**CROSS-CUTTING CONCLUSION**

The high school characteristics domain does not produce individual- level stratification of workforce outcomes among non-completers. Place-based context — community type, EDR, local wage level, and to a large extent local unemployment rate — does not determine which refined workforce participation category a non-completer enters or how their trajectory evolves over five years. The meaningful variation in outcomes documented in the demographic and high school accomplishments domains is driven by individual-level characteristics, not by where within Southeast Minnesota a graduate attended high school. The one exception — the unemployment rate push dynamic toward out-of-region sustained employment — is a structural labor market finding rather than evidence that place predicts individual disadvantage.

<br>

### `Dem_Desc`

OVERVIEW AND EFFECT SIZE

Community type (Dem_Desc) shows a small but statistically significant and gradually growing association with refined workforce participation outcomes across all five years (V=0.030, 0.030, 0.033, 0.037, 0.040 at Years 1–5). The effect size nearly doubles from Year 1 to Year 5, making Dem_Desc the only high school characteristics variable that strengthens meaningfully over time. Nevertheless, practical differences across the three community types remain small throughout.

SUSTAINED WF — REGION

Entirely urban graduates show the highest sustained regional employment at every time point, and urban/town/rural mix graduates show the lowest. At Year 1: 26.0% entirely urban vs. 25.3% town/rural mix vs. 24.0% urban/town/rural mix. The gap grows modestly over time: Year 5 (32.9% vs. 31.4% vs. 28.7%). By Year 5 the entirely urban to urban/town/rural mix gap reaches 4.2 percentage points — modest but the largest community type differential in the analysis. Urban graduates' higher sustained regional employment likely reflects their proximity to denser local labor markets with more employer access.

SUSTAINED WF — MN (OUT OF REGION)

Out-of-region sustained employment shows a consistent but small reversed gradient — urban/town/rural mix graduates show somewhat higher rates than entirely urban graduates at most time points. At Year 5: 16.5% urban/town/rural mix vs. 15.6% town/rural mix vs. 13.3% entirely urban. This likely reflects the broader geographic catchment areas of mixed community graduates who may have stronger ties to multiple labor markets within and beyond the region.

IN-REGION MARGINAL EMPLOYMENT AND OTHER DISCONNECTED EMPLOYMENT

Both non-sustained employment categories show differences of 2 percentage points or less across community types at every time point, with no consistent directional gradient. Community type does not meaningfully differentiate in-region marginal or other disconnected employment.

NO MN EMPLOYMENT RECORD

Urban/town/rural mix graduates are consistently overrepresented in the no MN employment record category, and this is the primary driver of the growing effect size over time. At Year 1: 27.6% urban/town/ rural mix vs. 24.9% town/rural mix vs. 23.7% entirely urban. At Year 5: 31.8% vs. 29.9% vs. 29.1%. The 2.7 point gap between the highest and lowest community types at Year 5 suggests that graduates from more geographically dispersed communities are modestly more likely to leave or remain absent from the Minnesota labor market over time.

TRAJECTORY SUMMARY

Dem_Desc shows a small but growing association driven primarily by two findings: entirely urban graduates have a modest advantage in sustained regional employment that accumulates over time, and urban/town/rural mix graduates are consistently more likely to have no Minnesota employment record. Neither difference rises to practical significance for policy purposes. Community type remains a weak predictor of refined workforce participation outcomes, and its gradual strengthening over five years reflects slow accumulation of small distributional differences rather than a meaningful structural effect.

### `edr`

OVERVIEW AND EFFECT SIZE

EDR shows no significant association with refined workforce participation outcomes in Years 1 and 2 (V=0.012, p=.322; V=0.016, p=.064). The association becomes statistically significant beginning at Year 3 but remains negligible in practical terms throughout (V=0.019, 0.029, 0.034 at Years 3–5). This is the weakest association in the entire high school characteristics group and confirms the consistent finding across prior analyses that EDR has no meaningful independent relationship with workforce outcomes for non-completers.

SUSTAINED WF — REGION

Regional sustained employment rates are nearly identical across EDR 9 and EDR 10 at every time point. At Year 1: 24.8% (EDR 10) vs. 25.1% (EDR 9) — a 0.3 point difference. By Year 5: 30.1% vs. 31.5% — a 1.4 point gap that, while slightly larger, is substantively trivial. EDR does not differentiate sustained regional employment rates at any point in the five-year window.

SUSTAINED WF — MN (OUT OF REGION)

Out-of-region sustained employment rates are also essentially identical across EDRs throughout. At Year 1: 9.7% vs. 9.9%. By Year 5: 14.8% vs. 16.6% — a 1.8 point gap, the largest EDR differential observed anywhere in the five-year analysis, and still negligible in magnitude.

IN-REGION MARGINAL EMPLOYMENT AND OTHER DISCONNECTED EMPLOYMENT

Both non-sustained employment categories show differences of 1 percentage point or less across EDRs at every time point. These differences are substantively meaningless and show no consistent directional pattern.

NO MN EMPLOYMENT RECORD

No-record rates show the largest EDR differences in the later years — 31.4% for EDR 10 vs. 28.7% for EDR 9 at Year 5. This 2.7 point gap likely reflects EDR 10's slightly larger geographic footprint and more rural composition rather than any meaningful structural difference in workforce outcomes. It is the primary driver of the late-emerging chi-square significance but carries no practical interpretive weight.

TRAJECTORY SUMMARY

EDR is effectively a null predictor of refined workforce participation outcomes at every time point. The late-emerging statistical significance at Years 3–5 is an artifact of sample size and small accumulated distributional differences rather than a meaningful place-based effect. Where a non-completer attended high school — whether in EDR 9 or EDR 10 — has no bearing on their workforce participation trajectory across the five-year window.

### `avg.unemp.rate`

OVERVIEW AND EFFECT SIZE

Average local unemployment rate is the strongest variable in the high school characteristics group and the only one with consistent statistical significance and meaningful pairwise differentiation across all five years (F=17.8, 11.4, 10.7, 14.8, 14.7 at Years 1–5). The omnibus association is significant throughout, though the pairwise structure shifts substantially across years in ways that are analytically informative.

SUSTAINED WF — REGION VS. OTHER CATEGORIES

At Year 1, graduates in sustained regional employment come from communities with meaningfully lower average unemployment than those in no MN employment record (difference=+0.172, p\<.001), other disconnected employment (difference=+0.112, p\<.001), sustained MN employment (difference=+0.091, p=.011), and in-region marginal employment (difference=+0.066, p=.025). The sustained regional employment group is associated with the lowest local unemployment rates, and the no-record group is associated with the highest — a gradient that runs from attachment to absence.

By Year 2, the contrast between sustained WF — Region and in-region marginal employment becomes non-significant (difference=+0.001, p=1.000), while the contrast with sustained WF — MN grows (difference=+0.134, p\<.001). From Year 2 onward, sustained MN employment is consistently associated with significantly higher local unemployment than sustained regional employment (Years 2–5 all p\<.001), with differences growing from 0.134 to 0.153. This is a stable and interpretively important finding: graduates who achieve sustained employment outside the region but within Minnesota come from communities with higher local unemployment — consistent with the interpretation that out-of-region sustained employment reflects labor market push factors rather than pull.

By Years 3–5, the no-record group is no longer significantly different from sustained regional employment (Year 5 p=.999), while sustained MN employment remains the most distinctive category. In-region marginal employment is significantly lower in local unemployment than sustained MN employment at Years 3–5 (differences of −0.135 to −0.185, all p\<.001) — meaning in-region marginal workers come from lower-unemployment communities than those who leave for sustained employment elsewhere in Minnesota.

TRAJECTORY SUMMARY

The local unemployment rate finding evolves meaningfully over the five-year window. In Year 1, it distinguishes labor market entrants broadly — those in sustained regional employment come from lower- unemployment communities, those with no record come from higher- unemployment communities. By Years 3–5, the primary and most robust contrast is between sustained out-of-region employment (higher local unemployment) and in-region employment of any kind (lower local unemployment). This suggests that local unemployment rate is less a predictor of individual outcomes than a contextual push factor — graduates from higher-unemployment communities are more likely to seek and achieve sustained employment outside the region. This is the most substantively interesting finding in the high school characteristics domain.

::: panel-tabset

### `avg.wages.pct.state`

OVERVIEW AND EFFECT SIZE

Average local wages as a percent of the state average is a consistent null predictor of refined workforce participation outcomes across the five-year window. The omnibus ANOVA is non-significant at Years 1 through 4 (p=.514, .245, .074, .187) and reaches marginal significance only at Year 5 (F=3.6, p=.006). No pairwise Tukey contrast is significant at Years 1–4. At Year 5, the only contrasts that reach significance are between sustained WF — MN and both other disconnected employment (difference=+0.005, p=.010) and no MN employment record (difference=+0.004, p=.011) — differences so small in absolute terms (fractions of a percentage point of the state wage average) as to carry no practical meaning.

This variable adds no analytical value to the characterization of refined workforce participation outcomes at any time point. Local wage level of the community where a graduate attended high school does not differentiate which outcome category non-completers enter, nor how their trajectory evolves over five years. This confirms the consistent null finding for this variable across all prior analytical frameworks in this study.

```{r}
saveWorkbook(wb, "Data/Claude/analysis_non_college_deeper/Refined disconnection/High school characteristics/avg-wages-pct-state-5.xlsx", overwrite = TRUE)
```
